name: Karl Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a usual working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl Moreau, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines since my certificate and apprenticeship. I know the water-tower span and its two close feeders, and I like getting a difficult fault right; I use the approved AI note helper occasionally, only after another worker showed me how.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tablet once showed the wrong feeder in rain. The printed sheet and meter reading settled it before our crew started work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster note is welcome after a long repair, but the wire still needs a measured check. A paper circuit number has saved us more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, a small change sounds comfortable. My line wage is ordinary, we've set aside about three months of expenses, and Eva's bakery work is steady enough that the rent is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking my normal crew shifts and use the approved note assistant now and then, as I do after messy repairs. In the first year I'll compare its output with the signed circuit sheet and leave our usual savings payment in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm. Our grown children have their own homes now, and Eva and I can enjoy a quiet evening after a callout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which paper number helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The water-tower span has two feeders close together, and the tablet showed the wrong one during a storm. Our printed sheet and a meter check kept us on the right line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using the assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A younger colleague showed me an approved way to shorten notes, and I waited until the supervisor said it was acceptable. I don't ask software to approve a switch.

say: I'd welcome **shorter notes** after long line repairs.
I'd keep **measured checks** and printed circuit numbers on site.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and two current wages make a small change manageable.
I still treat **software suggestions** as notes, not safety approval.
do: Keep **normal crew shifts** and continue regular savings payments.
Use the **approved note assistant** occasionally after repairs and compare output with signed sheets.
feel: **Calm** about income and daily field work.
S0.quote: I don't ask software to approve a switch.
fieldNote: Karl's **occasional AI use** began after peer demonstration and supervisor approval, fitting his measured approach.
His **three-month cushion** and Eva's bakery wage support calm, while the water-tower feeder mistake keeps him careful.

steps.text: Continue normal paid crew shifts and regular savings transfers
Use the approved assistant for completed repair notes checked against circuit sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot to let dispatchers and line crews test new routes before promising faster callouts. Buying software could help with fittings, but the stock clerk knows when a shelf count is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pole work should continue, and Eva still needs to bake and serve people, so our base wages look safe for now. I do think the utility could run tighter crews and offer fewer weekend callouts, which would make the three-month buffer harder to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask to join the approved route trial once dispatchers have tested it, and I'd log every wrong water-tower feeder suggestion. In the first year Eva and I would put off replacing the kitchen table if callout pay drops, while I keep my regular line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about a tool that saves a real drive and uneasy about the extra pay. I don't want the office workers made invisible when they catch a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two feeder labels, the suggested route and the meter reading after we arrive. If the tool repeats the error, dispatch should see a dated example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The current table has a cracked edge but still stands. A new one can wait if overtime gets thin.

say: I'd ask for **crew-tested routes** before faster callouts are promised.
I'd defend **stock clerk checks** on actual fittings.
think: Our **base wages** look safe while robots spread slowly.
Fewer **weekend callouts** could slow our savings and tighten the household budget.
do: Join the **approved route trial** after dispatch testing and log feeder errors.
Keep **regular line shifts** and delay the table if callout income falls.
feel: **Curious** about the tool, uneasy about extra pay.
S1.quote: If the tool repeats the error, dispatch should see a dated example.
fieldNote: Karl expects **physical wages to continue** but sees a plausible near-term reduction in callouts and savings growth.
His **route log** records feeder labels and meter readings, giving dispatch concrete evidence instead of general complaints.

steps.text: Use the approved route tool and log water-tower feeder mistakes
Continue regular paid line shifts during scheduling changes
Delay replacing the kitchen table if callout pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 may change our permits and buying, but field robots around 2031 could take repairs. We should test machines with workers present and bargain for paid retraining before anyone loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots can do the hands-on work, and I might still need my wage. Eva's bakery job could face capable machines too; three months saved and some nearby utilities give us options, not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union for a worker-led robot trial and a paid course in inspecting completed repairs. In 2029 I'd enroll if the employer covers wages and fees; during the first robot year I'd apply for posted inspection shifts here and at the utilities within driving distance, keeping my crew hours while available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about two practical jobs changing together. I can learn a proven method. The new roles may be fewer than the workers who want them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test in that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the robot to distinguish the water-tower feeders in rain and to stop if the readings disagree. A crew should sign the trial report before any regular deployment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Eva?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Eva we should keep the three-month reserve for bills while I apply. Our grown children have their own rent and shouldn't be our fallback income.

say: I'd separate **2028 permit AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd seek **worker-led trials** and paid retraining before shift cuts.
think: At **63**, I may still need line wages when robots repair faults.
Eva's **bakery income** could also face machines, so three months saved is limited.
do: Ask the **union** for worker-led trials and paid inspection training now.
Enroll if **fees and wages** are covered in 2029, then apply for posted inspection shifts in 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about two wages, with some nearby work to pursue.
S2.quote: The new roles may be fewer than the workers who want them.
fieldNote: Karl places **job risk**, while the earlier thinking system changes permits and buying.
His **training requirement** includes wages and fees, and his local applications are real searches rather than guaranteed replacements.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate worker-led robot trials and paid training
Enroll in inspection training in 2029 if fees and wages are covered
Apply for posted inspection shifts at reachable utilities in 2031
Keep paid crew shifts during the inspection job search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers five years is long enough to run rain trials and tell workers which safety jobs will actually be paid. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement at 66 might be possible, but I don't know the real income until Eva and I see the statements. Bakery work could also change around 2034, and our three-month reserve wouldn't cover a long mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request written retirement forecasts for both of us and offer the water-tower feeder notes to a union safety group. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection placement if the trial produces one; in 2034 I'd compare posted wages with retirement income and choose continued paid work if bills require it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less hurried and still careful. The extra years give us room to test the machine and our own budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the trial report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot should stop when a feeder label and meter reading disagree, especially in rain. I want a crew signature and the failures counted beside successful calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What costs would decide retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing, Eva's medicines and the bakery's slow weeks. We can't use my partner Eva's busiest holiday season as the year-round figure.

say: I'd ask for **rain trials** and real paid safety roles.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from 2034 field robots.
think: Retirement at **66** depends on both income statements and slow bakery weeks.
A **three-month reserve** cannot cover a long income error.
do: Get **retirement forecasts** and share water-tower notes with the union group.
Take a **paid placement** if offered in 2032; compare posted wages with retirement in 2034.
feel: **Less hurried**, with caution about the household budget.
S3.quote: We can't use my partner Eva's busiest holiday season as the year-round figure.
fieldNote: Karl's **2034 choice** depends on conservative bakery income and verified retirement statements for both partners.
His **trial criterion** pairs a disagreeing meter reading with a stop rule and crew signature.

steps.text: Compare both retirement statements with housing and slow bakery weeks
Share water-tower fault notes with the union safety group
Take a paid inspection placement in 2032 if offered
Apply for posted safety work if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell newer crews ten years is time to record every old feeder and train people to check a machine's work. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect I could retire before 71 if the written figures cover us. Eva's bakery work might change before then, so we need to use her slow-season pay in the budget rather than assume every week is busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid line shifts and request updated retirement forecasts every year. In 2037 Eva and I would set a date if housing and medicine fit; in 2039 I'd give the new crew the water-tower feeder notes and attend a union robot safety meeting if trial failures persist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own income over the next few years and concerned for workers who will still be on the rota. The extra time gives us a choice and a chance to leave good records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new crew learn from the notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two feeders sit close together, and the older label fades in rain. I'd mark the meter readings and the angle of the printed tag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures don't cover retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid line work if it remains and apply for a real inspection opening. I wouldn't expect our grown children to cover the gap.

say: I'd ask crews to record **old feeder details** and robot trial failures.
I'd name **2039 field robots** as the hands-on change when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** may work if written figures cover bills.
Eva's **slow bakery weeks** belong in the household forecast.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and update retirement forecasts annually.
Choose a **2037 date** if bills fit; pass feeder notes and join a union safety meeting in 2039.
feel: **Calm** about near-term income, concerned for later crews.
S4.quote: The extra time gives us a choice and a chance to leave good records.
fieldNote: Karl expects **retirement before 2039** to be possible with conservative figures, rather than assuming a guaranteed pension.
His **feeder notes** preserve a faded label and meter readings for crews and future robot safety review.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and update retirement forecasts each year
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if housing and medicine fit
Attend a union robot safety meeting in 2039 if failures persist

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because 2031 robots could reach both my line work and Eva's bakery job while we still need wages. Worker-led trials, paid inspection training, real posted jobs and honest retirement figures would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a robot stops when the meter reading disagrees with the label. A lineworker shouldn't be the first person to learn the stop rule after a fault.

headlineQuote: A lineworker shouldn't be the first person to learn the stop rule after a fault.
portrait: Karl is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, typical pay and about three months saved.
His **water-tower feeder error** makes him cautious with software, while Eva's bakery income supports the current household.
He uses **AI occasionally** after peer demonstration and backs route suggestions with signed sheets and meter readings.
The **2031 robot date** worries him because both hands-on jobs could change before retirement is affordable.
A longer runway supports **union safety trials** and written retirement checks while he keeps paid line shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Karl most because 2031 robots could affect both his repairs and Eva's bakery wage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **worker-led trials**, paid inspection training, posted jobs and reliable retirement figures.
